sentences.t:
oð þæt him on innan oferhygda dǣl
weaxeð ond wrīdað;
sentences.l: until within him a share of over-thoughts grows and thrives;
sentences.i: until a measure of pride swells and flourishes within him;
sentences.n: This opens in the middle of a sentence: it carries on the picture of the fortunate man at 1735–1739, who ‘wunað on wiste’ and ‘þæt wyrse ne con’, and ‘oð þæt’ means ‘until’. The lines are still Hrothgar’s speech, which began at 1700 in the last part, so there is no opening quotation mark here; Klaeber’s closing mark comes at 1784. ‘him on innan’ is ‘in him within’, ‘him’ a dative. ‘oferhygda dǣl’ is ‘a share of over-thoughts’ (‘oferhygd’, ‘pride, arrogance’, with ‘oferhygda’ a genitive plural), and it is the subject of both singular verbs, ‘weaxeð’ ‘grows’ and ‘wrīdað’, which I take from ‘wrīdan’, ‘flourish, thrive’. The man is the one whom God has let rise in the lines before.

sentences.t:
þonne se weard swefeð,
sāwele hyrde;
sentences.l: then the guardian sleeps, the keeper of the soul;
sentences.i: then the watchman sleeps, the keeper of the soul;
sentences.n: ‘þonne’ is ‘then’ (it can also mean ‘when’), picking up ‘oð þæt’ above. ‘weard’ is ‘guardian’, ‘swefeð’ the third person singular of ‘swefan’, ‘sleep’, and ‘sāwele hyrde’ is ‘keeper of the soul’, ‘sāwele’ a genitive singular and ‘hyrde’ a nominative in apposition to ‘weard’. Since the next lines bring in an arrow and an ‘accursed spirit’, I read him as the part of a man that should watch against such attacks, conscience or the will; that reading is mine, not stated.

sentences.t:
bið se slǣp tō fæst,
bisgum gebunden, bona swīðe nēah,
sē þe of flānbogan fyrenum scēoteð.
sentences.l: is the sleep too fast, bound with cares, the slayer very near, he who from the arrow-bow shoots wickedly.
sentences.i: The sleep is too deep, held fast by cares, and the slayer is very near, he who shoots wickedly from the bow.
sentences.n: ‘bið’ is the form of ‘bēon’, ‘be’, that says what is or comes to be, ‘is, becomes’. ‘tō fæst’ is ‘too fast’, ‘fæst’ ‘firm, fixed’, said of sleep, and ‘bisgum gebunden’ is ‘bound with cares’, ‘gebunden’ a past participle and ‘bisgum’ a dative plural of ‘bisgu’, ‘care, trouble’: the man’s own worries hold the guard asleep. ‘bona’ is ‘slayer’ and ‘swīðe nēah’ ‘very near’. ‘sē þe … scēoteð’ is ‘he who shoots’, ‘flānbogan’ the dative of ‘flānboga’, ‘arrow-bow’ (‘flān’ ‘arrow’), and ‘fyrenum’ a dative plural used as an adverb, ‘with wickedness, wickedly’. ‘wergan gāstes’ in 1747 suggests that the slayer is the accursed spirit, the devil; that reading is mine.

sentences.l: Then he is struck in the breast, beneath the helm, by a bitter arrow — to guard himself he knows not how —, with the wicked wonder-commands of the accursed ghast;
sentences.i: Then he is struck in the heart, beneath his helmet, by a bitter arrow — he does not know how to guard himself —, with the wicked, strange commands of the accursed spirit;
sentences.n: The subject of ‘bið … drepen’ (‘is struck’, a passive) is the man of the last lines, with no pronoun stated. ‘hreþre’ is the dative of ‘hreþer’, ‘breast, heart’, and ‘under helm’ ‘beneath the helmet’: the arrow goes in beneath the helmet. ‘biteran strǣle’ is a dative, ‘with a bitter arrow’. The dashes enclose ‘him bebeorgan ne con’, ‘he knows not how to guard himself’, ‘con’ the third person of ‘cunnan’ and ‘him’ a reflexive dative. ‘wōm’ is the hard word: the lexica give a noun for ‘stain, sin, wickedness’, and I read it as qualifying the commands, ‘wicked’, which is a guess at both word and form. ‘wundọrbebodum’ is a dative plural, ‘with wonder-commands’ (‘wundor’ ‘wonder, marvel, horror’ and ‘bebod’ ‘command’), the orders of ‘wergan gāstes’, ‘of the accursed ghast’, the phrase used of Grendel at 133 (‘wergan’ is the weak genitive of ‘wearg’, ‘accursed’). The dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘wundọrbebodum’ is Klaeber’s sign that this vowel does not count in the metre, and the same sign comes again at 1782 and 1797.

sentences.t:
þinceð him tō lȳtel, þæt hē lange hēold,
gȳtsað gromhȳdig, nallas on gylp seleð
fǣtte bēagas, ond hē þā forðgesceaft
forgyteð ond forgȳmeð, þæs þe him ǣr God sealde,
wuldres Waldend, weorðmynda dǣl.
sentences.l: It seems to him too little, what he long held; he covets, grim-minded, and gives not at all plated rings for glory, and he forgets and neglects the forth-decree, since God gave him before, glory’s Wielder, a share of honours.
sentences.i: What he has long held seems too little to him; he grows covetous and grim of mind, and gives no plated rings for the glory of it; and he forgets and neglects the fate ordained for him, because God, the Ruler of glory, had earlier given him a share of honours.
sentences.n: One sentence, about the man struck in 1745–1747. ‘þinceð him tō lȳtel’ is ‘it seems to him too little’, an impersonal verb with a dative, and ‘þæt hē lange hēold’ is ‘what he long held’; the apparatus records that the manuscript has ‘to’ before ‘lange’, ‘imperfectly erased’. ‘gȳtsað’ is ‘covets’ (from ‘gȳtsian’) and ‘gromhȳdig’ ‘grim-minded’. ‘nallas’ is ‘not at all’, ‘on gylp’ ‘for glory’ (‘gylp’ is ‘boast, glory’), and ‘fǣtte bēagas’ ‘plated rings’, the rings a king should hand out and this man keeps. Klaeber’s italic ‘tt’ in ‘fǣtte’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘fædde’, which does not suit ‘rings’ as it stands, and Thorpe’s ‘fǣtte’ is an accusative plural of the participle of ‘fǣtan’, ‘adorn’, ‘plated, adorned’; that sense is from the lexica and is partly a guess. ‘forðgesceaft’ is ‘forth-decree’ (‘forð’ ‘forth, onward’ and ‘gesceaft’ ‘creation, decree’), what is fixed to come for him, and it is the object of ‘forgyteð’ ‘forgets’ and ‘forgȳmeð’ ‘neglects’. ‘þæs þe him ǣr God sealde’ can be ‘since God had earlier given him’, which I follow, or ‘of that which God earlier gave him’, with ‘weorðmynda dǣl’ (‘a share of honours’) as the thing given. ‘wuldres Waldend’ is the house ‘glory’s Wielder’ (‘Ruler of glory’ in the idiomatic line), as at 183, ‘Waldend’ being the ‘Wielder’ of 1661. The apparatus marks the start of a new manuscript leaf (fol. 168b) at ‘waldend’, citing the sigla ‘AB’ (I take these to be the two Thorkelin transcripts).

sentences.l: In the end it comes about in turn that the body, fleeting, sinks, falls doomed;
sentences.i: In the end it comes about that the fleeting body fails and falls, doomed;
sentences.n: ‘Hit … gelimpeð’ is ‘it happens’, ‘hit’ a dummy subject and the ‘þæt’ clause saying what happens. ‘on endestæf’ is an idiom for ‘at the end’ (‘ende’ ‘end’ and ‘stæf’, ‘staff’ or ‘letter’; I do not know why, and take the phrase only as a unit), and ‘eft’ is ‘afterwards, in turn’. ‘līchoma’ is ‘body’ (‘līc’ ‘body’ and ‘hama’ ‘covering’, so the body as a garment); ‘lǣne’ is ‘fleeting’, from the same root as ‘lǣn’, ‘loan’, a thing lent only for a time. ‘gedrēoseð’ is the third person of ‘gedrēosan’, ‘sink, fail, fall’, ‘fǣge’ is ‘doomed to die’, and ‘gefealleð’ ‘falls’. The semicolon ends the picture of the dying man and the next unit tells what happens to his goods.

sentences.t:
fēhð ōþer tō,
sē þe unmurnlīce mādmas dǣleþ,
eorles ǣrgestrēon, egesan ne gȳmeð.
sentences.l: another takes over, who without mourning deals out the treasures, the earl’s ancient-wealth, and cares not for terror.
sentences.i: Another succeeds him, who shares out the treasures without regret, the earl’s old hoard, and gives no heed to terror.
sentences.n: ‘fēhð … tō’ is ‘takes over’: ‘fōn tō’ is the phrase for coming into an inheritance, and ‘ōþer’ is ‘another’, the heir. ‘sē þe unmurnlīce mādmas dǣleþ’ is ‘who without mourning deals out treasures’; ‘unmurnlīce’ is ‘without care or regret’ (‘murnan’ ‘mourn, be anxious’), so he gives away freely what the miser kept, and ‘mādmas’ is a spelling of ‘māþmas’, ‘treasures’. ‘eorles ǣrgestrēon’ is ‘the earl’s ancient wealth’, in apposition (‘ǣr-’ ‘earlier’ and ‘gestrēon’ ‘acquisition, wealth’), the dead man’s long-gathered store. ‘egesan ne gȳmeð’ is ‘does not heed terror’, ‘gȳman’ ‘heed, care for’ taking a genitive or accusative; whether this means that the heir has no fear, or no awe of the dead man, the text does not say, and my rendering is a guess.

sentences.l: Guard yourself against that bale-malice, dear Beowulf, best of men, and choose for yourself the better, eternal counsels;
sentences.i: Guard yourself against that baleful malice, dear Beowulf, best of men, and choose what is better, the lasting gains;
sentences.n: Here Hrothgar turns from the general man to Beowulf. ‘Bebeorh’ is the imperative of ‘bebeorgan’, ‘guard against’, with the reflexive dative ‘þē’ (‘yourself’) and ‘ðone bealonīð’ as what is guarded against: ‘bealu’ is ‘evil, bale’ and ‘nīð’ ‘hatred, hostile act’, so the malice of the arrow and the pride just described. ‘Bēowulf lēofa’ is a vocative with the weak adjective, ‘dear Beowulf’, as at 1216. ‘secg[a] betsta’ is ‘best of men’, ‘secga’ a genitive plural and ‘betsta’ a superlative; the bracketed ‘a’ is Klaeber’s addition to the manuscript’s ‘secg’, which Thorpe (in Kemble), Sievers and four other editors also make, while Grundtvig and Heyne repair it as ‘secg [se] betsta’, ‘man, the best’ (the apparatus refers to the note on 947a). ‘þē þæt sēlre gecēos’ is ‘choose for yourself the better’, ‘gecēos’ the imperative of ‘gecēosan’, ‘choose’, and ‘þæt sēlre’ a neuter comparative used as a noun. ‘ēce rǣdas’ is ‘eternal counsels’, an accusative plural in apposition; ‘rǣd’ may mean ‘advantage, benefit’ rather than ‘advice’ here, and that choice is a guess. The semicolon sets off a second command.

sentences.t:
oferhȳda ne gȳm,
mǣre cempa!
sentences.l: Of over-thoughts take no heed, famed champion!
sentences.i: Take no heed of pride, famed champion!
sentences.n: ‘oferhȳda’ is a genitive plural of the noun that appears as ‘oferhygda’ at 1740, in a spelling with ‘ȳ’; the word returns to name what the lines about the fallen man were about. ‘ne gȳm’ is the imperative of ‘gȳman’ with ‘ne’, ‘do not heed’, here with a genitive (at 1757 ‘egesan’ may be a genitive or an accusative). ‘mǣre cempa’ is a vocative, ‘famed champion’ (‘cempa’ ‘fighter’).

sentences.t:
Nū is þīnes mægnes blǣd
āne hwīle;
sentences.l: Now the bloom of your might is for a single while;
sentences.i: Now your strength is in its bloom, but only for a while;
sentences.n: ‘blǣd’ is ‘bloom, glory’, the word used of Beowulf’s fame at 1703, here the flowering of strength, and ‘þīnes mægnes’ is a genitive, ‘of your might’. ‘āne hwīle’ is an accusative of time, ‘for a single while’, ‘āne’ ‘one, only’. The semicolon sets the short time against what follows.

sentences.t:
eft sōna bið,
þæt þec ādl oððe ecg eafoþes getwǣfeð,
oððe fȳres feng, oððe flōdes wylm,
oððe gripe mēces, oððe gāres fliht,
oððe atol yldo;
sentences.l: afterwards soon it will be that sickness or blade will part you from strength, or fire’s clutch, or flood’s surge, or sword’s grip, or spear’s flight, or dread old age;
sentences.i: Before long it will come about that sickness or the blade cuts you off from your strength — or the clutch of fire, or the surge of flood, or the grip of a sword, or the flight of a spear, or dreadful old age;
sentences.n: ‘eft sōna’ is ‘soon after’ and ‘bið’ ‘will be’, the present of ‘bēon’ used for the future, introducing the ‘þæt’ clause. ‘getwǣfeð’ is ‘parts, cuts off’ (the verb of ‘getwǣfed’ at 1658), with ‘þec’, the older accusative ‘you’ (like ‘mec’), as the person parted and ‘eafoþes’, a genitive, as what he is parted from: ‘from strength’. The one singular verb serves a string of subjects joined by ‘oððe’, ‘or’: ‘ādl’ ‘sickness’, ‘ecg’ ‘edge, blade’, ‘fȳres feng’ ‘the clutch of fire’ (‘feng’ ‘grasp’), ‘flōdes wylm’ ‘the surge of flood’, ‘gripe mēces’ ‘the grip of a sword’, ‘gāres fliht’ ‘the flight of a spear’ and ‘atol yldo’ ‘dreadful age’. The semicolon after ‘yldo’ closes this list, and a last cause follows.

sentences.t:
oððe ēagena bearhtm
forsiteð ond forsworceð;
sentences.l: or the brightness of the eyes obstructs and darkens;
sentences.i: or the brightness of your eyes clouds over and grows dim;
sentences.n: ‘ēagena bearhtm’ is ‘the brightness of the eyes’ (‘bearhtm’ ‘flash, brightness’, ‘ēagena’ a genitive plural), the last of the causes, and the subject of both verbs. ‘forsworceð’ is ‘grows dark’ (‘forsweorcan’, ‘become dark’). ‘forsiteð’ I take as ‘obstructs, clogs’, from ‘forsittan’ (‘hinder’); the pair means that sight fails and darkens, and the sense of the first verb is a guess from its parts. The semicolon closes the list.

sentences.t:
semninga bið,
þæt ðec, dryhtguma, dēað oferswȳðeð.
sentences.l: suddenly it will be that death will overpower you, troop-man.
sentences.i: Suddenly it will come about that death overpowers you, warrior.
sentences.n: ‘semninga’ ‘suddenly’ and ‘bið’ ‘will be’ introduce a second ‘þæt’ clause, again with ‘ðec’, the old accusative ‘you’. ‘dryhtguma’ is a vocative, ‘troop-man’ (‘dryht’ ‘troop, company’ and ‘guma’ ‘man’), a warrior of a lord’s company. ‘oferswȳðeð’ is the third person of ‘oferswȳðan’, ‘overpower’, and ‘dēað’ its subject. The list before gave the means one by one; this clause names only death itself, and ‘semninga’ says it comes without warning.

sentences.t:
Swā ic Hring-Dena hund missēra
wēold under wolcnum ond hig wigge belēac
manigum mǣgþa geond þysne middangeard,
æscum ond ecgum, þæt ic mē ǣnigne
under swegles begong gesacan ne tealde.
sentences.l: So I ruled the Ring-Danes a hundred half-years under the clouds, and shut them in with war against many of the tribes throughout this middle-yard, with ash-spears and edges, so that I reckoned no adversary for myself under the circuit of the sky.
sentences.i: So I ruled the Ring-Danes for a hundred seasons under the heavens, and kept them safe by war from many of the tribes throughout this middle-earth, with spear and sword, so that I counted no one under the whole round of the sky my enemy.
sentences.n: ‘Swā’ is ‘so, thus’ and begins Hrothgar’s account of himself as the example. ‘Hring-Dena’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the Ring-Danes’ (as ‘Hring-Dene’ at 116), the object of ‘wēold’, because ‘wealdan’ takes the genitive. ‘hund missēra’ is the formula of 1498, said there of the mere-woman, ‘a hundred half-years’, an accusative of time: ‘missēra’ is ‘half-year, season’, so the span is fifty years or a hundred, and I cannot tell which; that reading is a guess. ‘under wolcnum’ is ‘under the clouds’, a dative plural. ‘ond hig wigge belēac’ is ‘and shut them in with war’: ‘hig’ is ‘them’ (the Danes), ‘wigge’ a dative, ‘with war’, and ‘belēac’ the past of ‘belūcan’, ‘lock, enclose’. With ‘manigum mǣgþa’ (‘many of the tribes’, a dative plural with a genitive plural) I take the sense ‘protected them by war against many peoples’, which is a guess at the construction. ‘middangeard’ is ‘middle-yard’, the inhabited earth, as at 75 and, in the genitive, 751. ‘æscum ond ecgum’ is ‘with ash-spears and edges’: ‘æsc’ ‘ash-wood’ stands for the spear and ‘ecg’ ‘edge’ for the sword. The ‘þæt’ clause gives the result: ‘ic mē ǣnigne … gesacan ne tealde’ is ‘I reckoned no adversary for myself’, ‘ǣnigne’ ‘any’, ‘gesacan’ an accusative singular of ‘gesaca’, ‘adversary’, and ‘under swegles begong’ is ‘under the circuit of the sky’ (‘swegel’ ‘sky’ and ‘begong’ ‘circuit’, as in ‘flōda begong’ at 1497).

sentences.l: What! To me for that came a turn-about in the homeland, sorrow after joy, since Grendel became, the old foe, my in-goer;
sentences.i: Listen! Because of that, a reversal came upon me in my own land, grief after gladness, once Grendel had become my old enemy and my intruder;
sentences.n: ‘Hwæt’ is the house ‘What!’ (‘Listen!’). ‘edwenden’ is ‘turn-about, reversal’ (‘ed-’ ‘back, again’ and ‘wenden’ ‘turning’), the subject of ‘cwōm’, ‘came’, with ‘mē’ a dative ‘to me’, ‘þæs’ a genitive ‘for that’, and ‘on ēþle’ ‘in the homeland’. Klaeber’s italic ‘e’ in ‘edwenden’ marks a change: the manuscript has ‘ed wendan’, as two words, and the editors named in the apparatus (Grein, Sprachschatz, and most others) join them and read ‘-wenden’; it refers to the note on 280a, where the same word stands. ‘gyrn æfter gomene’ is ‘sorrow after joy’, in apposition. ‘seoþðan Grendel wearð’ is ‘since Grendel became’, with ‘ealdgewinna’ (‘old foe’: ‘eald’ ‘old’ and ‘gewinna’ ‘one who strives’) and ‘ingenga mīn’ (‘my in-goer’, an intruder: ‘in’ and ‘genga’ ‘goer’) as what he became. Thorpe, Grein and Grundtvig print ‘eald gewinna’ as two words, with the same sense.

sentences.t:
ic þǣre sōcne singāles wæg
mōdceare micle.
sentences.l: I bore for that attack, continually, great mind-care.
sentences.i: Because of that assault I bore great sorrow of heart without ceasing.
sentences.n: A new manuscript leaf (fol. 169a) begins at ‘ic’. ‘wæg’ is the past of ‘wegan’, ‘bear, carry’, with ‘mōdceare micle’ (‘great mind-care’: ‘mōd’ ‘mind, spirit’ and ‘cearu’ ‘sorrow’) as its object, ‘singāles’ ‘continually’ a genitive used as an adverb, and ‘þǣre sōcne’ a dative, ‘because of that attack’; ‘sōcn’ is ‘attack, pursuit’ and here means Grendel’s visits. The length of the affliction is given at 147, ‘twelve winters’.

sentences.t:
Þæs sig Metode þanc,
ēcean Dryhtne, þæs ðe ic on aldre gebād,
þæt ic on þone hafelan heorodrēorigne
ofer eald gewin ēagum starige!
sentences.l: For that be thanks to the Measurer, the eternal Lord, for that which I lived to see in my life, that I on the head, sword-gory, after the old strife may stare with my eyes!
sentences.i: Thanks be to God, the eternal Lord, for this and for what I have lived to see in my life: that after the old strife I may gaze with my own eyes on that blood-stained head!
sentences.n: ‘Þæs sig Metode þanc’ is ‘for that be thanks to the Measurer’: ‘sig’ is the present subjunctive of ‘wesan’, ‘be’ (a wish, ‘let there be’), ‘Metode’ a dative, the house ‘Measurer’ (‘God’ in the idiomatic line), and ‘ēcean Dryhtne’ ‘to the eternal Lord’ beside it, the phrase of 1692. ‘þæs ðe ic on aldre gebād’ is ‘for that which I lived to see in my life’: ‘gebād’ is the past of ‘gebīdan’, ‘live to see, experience’ (as at 1720), and ‘on aldre’ ‘in life’. The ‘þæt’ clause says what: ‘þæt ic … ēagum starige’, ‘that I may stare with my eyes’, ‘starige’ a present subjunctive of ‘starian’, ‘stare’. ‘on þone hafelan’ is ‘on the head’, and the head is Grendel’s, which Beowulf has brought to the hall. ‘heorodrēorigne’ is ‘sword-gory’ (‘drēorig’ ‘bloody, gory’, with ‘heoro-’ ‘sword’); as with ‘heorogīfre’ at 1498 the prefix may only intensify, so ‘sword-’ is a guess. ‘ofer eald gewin’ is ‘after the old strife’, ‘ofer’ in the sense ‘beyond, after’, the strife being the twelve years of 147; Holthausen joins it as one word, ‘ealdgewinnan’. The exclamation mark is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
Gā nū tō setle, symbẹlwynne drēoh
wīggeweorþad;
sentences.l: Go now to the seat, enjoy feast-joy, war-honoured;
sentences.i: Go now to your seat, honoured in war, and enjoy the pleasure of the feast;
sentences.n: ‘Gā’ is the imperative of ‘gān’, ‘go’, ‘tō setle’ ‘to the seat’, and ‘drēoh’ the imperative of ‘drēogan’, ‘carry out, enjoy’. ‘symbẹlwynne’ is ‘feast-joy’ (‘symbel’ ‘feast’ and ‘wynn’ ‘joy’), the object; the dot under the ‘ẹ’ is the metrical sign met at 1747, and Sievers and Holthausen print the word without the final ‘e’, ‘symbelwynn’ (the apparatus refers to the Language section § 20.2). ‘wīggeweorþad’ is ‘war-honoured’, a past participle agreeing with the ‘you’ addressed, ‘made worthy by war’. The manuscript has it as two words, ‘wigge weorþad’; Holthausen and Sedgefield read ‘wigge geweorþad’ (with the prefix ‘ge-’), and Kemble and others print the compound as Klaeber does. The semicolon begins the promise.

sentences.t:
unc sceal worn fela
māþma gemǣnra, siþðan morgen bið.’
sentences.l: for us two shall be a great many of treasures in common, when morning is.’
sentences.i: We two shall have many treasures in common when morning comes.’
sentences.n: ‘unc’ is the dual dative ‘to us two’ (the dual, as ‘wit’ at 1707), and ‘sceal’ ‘shall’ has no infinitive stated; ‘be’ or ‘come’ is understood, as often after ‘sculan’. ‘worn fela’ is ‘a great many’, with ‘māþma’ a partitive genitive plural, ‘of treasures’, and ‘gemǣnra’ a genitive plural, ‘common, shared’; the apparatus records Kock’s ‘gemǣne’ in place of ‘gemǣnra’. ‘siþðan morgen bið’ is ‘when morning is’, ‘siþðan’ ‘when, after’ and ‘bið’ the future. The mark ’ after ‘bið.’ is Klaeber’s closing quotation mark: it ends Hrothgar’s speech, which began at 1700.

sentences.t:
Gēat wæs glædmōd, gēong sōna tō,
setles nēosan, swā se snottra heht.
sentences.l: The Geat was glad-minded, went soon thereto, to seek the seat, as the wise one bade.
sentences.i: The Geat was glad at heart and went at once to find his seat, as the wise one had bidden.
sentences.n: ‘Gēat’ is ‘the Geat’, Beowulf, who is named here only by his people. ‘glædmōd’ is ‘glad-minded’. ‘gēong’ is the past of ‘gongan’, ‘go’, with ‘sōna tō’ ‘at once thereto’ (‘tō’ an adverb) and ‘setles nēosan’ ‘to seek the seat’, an infinitive of purpose after a verb of motion, ‘nēosan’ taking ‘setles’ as a genitive. ‘se snottra’ is ‘the wise one’, Hrothgar, who has just spoken, and ‘heht’ the past of ‘hātan’, ‘bid’. Hrothgar’s command at 1782 was ‘Gā nū tō setle’, and Beowulf does that.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs eft swā ǣr ellenrōfum,
fletsittendum fægere gereorded
nīowan stefne. —
sentences.l: Then it was again, as before, fairly feasted for the courage-strong ones, the hall-sitters, with a new turn. —
sentences.i: Then once more, as before, a fine meal was served to the brave men who sat in the hall, a fresh round of feasting. —
sentences.n: ‘gereorded’ is a past participle of ‘gereordan’, ‘feed, provide a meal’, and ‘wæs … gereorded’ an impersonal passive, ‘a meal was served’, with ‘ellenrōfum’ (‘courage-strong ones’: ‘ellen’ ‘courage’ and ‘rōf’ ‘strong, bold’) and ‘fletsittendum’ (‘hall-sitters’: ‘flet’ ‘floor, hall’ and ‘sittend’ ‘sitter’) as datives of the people served. ‘eft swā ǣr’ is ‘again as before’, and ‘fægere’ ‘fairly, well’. ‘nīowan stefne’ is a dative: ‘stefn’ means ‘voice’ and also ‘time, turn’, and the phrase is read ‘anew, a second time’; that sense is a guess. Klaeber ends the sentence with a full stop and adds a dash, which here marks a change of scene from the feast to the night.

sentences.t:
Nihthelm geswearc
deorc ofer dryhtgumum.
sentences.l: Night-helm grew dark, dark over the troop-men.
sentences.i: The helm of night grew dark, gloomy above the warriors.
sentences.n: ‘Nihthelm’ is ‘night-helm’, the covering of night (‘helm’ ‘covering, protection’, the word in ‘heofena Helm’, ‘Helm of the heavens’, at 182, and the night-covering ‘scaduhelma’, ‘shadow-helms’, at 650), ‘geswearc’ the past of ‘sweorcan’, ‘grow dark’, with the prefix ‘ge-’, and ‘deorc’ ‘dark’, an adjective after the verb. ‘ofer dryhtgumum’ is ‘over the troop-men’, ‘dryhtgumum’ a dative plural of the word that is the vocative ‘dryhtguma’ at 1768.

sentences.l: The proven warriors all rose up; the blended-haired one wished to seek his bed, the old Scylding.
sentences.i: The whole company of seasoned warriors rose; the grey-haired king wished to go to his bed, the aged Scylding.
sentences.n: ‘Duguð’ is the body of tried warriors, set against ‘iogoþ’, the young, in ‘duguðe ond iogoþe’ at 1674; it is a collective noun taking the singular verb ‘ārās’, the past of ‘ārīsan’, ‘rise’, with ‘eal’ ‘all’. ‘wolde … nēosan’ is ‘wished to seek’, ‘beddes’ a genitive after ‘nēosan’. ‘blondenfeax’ is ‘blended-haired’ (‘blonden’, the participle of ‘blandan’, ‘mix’, and ‘feax’ ‘hair’), which I take as hair mixed with grey, and ‘gamela Scylding’ is ‘the old Scylding’, a descendant of Scyld and a name for the Danes’ king. He is Hrothgar, who spoke the last lines and was called ‘se snottra’ at 1786.

sentences.t:
Gēat unigmetes wēl,
rōfne randwigan restan lyste;
sentences.l: The Geat, immeasurably well, the bold shield-warrior it pleased to rest;
sentences.i: The Geat was exceedingly content; it pleased that bold shield-warrior to rest;
sentences.n: ‘unigmetes’ is ‘beyond measure, exceedingly’, with ‘wēl’ ‘well’, so ‘very well (pleased)’. The manuscript spelling, divided across a line there, is ‘unig/metes’ and Klaeber keeps it; Thorpe and others print ‘ungemetes’ and ‘ungimetes’ is given under the apparatus siglum ‘E.’ (I take that to be Earle, but the packet does not spell it out) (the apparatus refers to the Language section § 18.8). The construction shifts: ‘Gēat’ is a nominative at the head of the line, but ‘restan lyste’ is the impersonal ‘it pleased (him) to rest’, ‘lystan’ taking the accusative of the person, and that person is ‘rōfne randwigan’, ‘the bold shield-warrior’ (‘rand’ ‘shield-rim’ and ‘wiga’ ‘warrior’), the same man as ‘Gēat’. I read ‘Gēat unigmetes wēl’ as a half-line standing alone, ‘the Geat, exceedingly well (content)’.

sentences.t:
sōna him seleþegn sīðes wērgum,
feorrancundum forð wīsade,
sē for andrysnum ealle beweotede
þegnes þearfe, swylce þȳ dōgọre
heaþolīðende habban scoldon.
sentences.l: Soon the hall-thane guided forth him, weary of the journey, come from afar — he who out of courtesies attended to all a thane’s need, such as battle-sailers on that day had to have.
sentences.i: At once the hall-thane led him on, weary from the journey and come from afar; out of courtesy he saw to every need a thane could have, such as seafaring warriors would then require.
sentences.n: ‘him’ is a dative, ‘sīðes wērgum’ ‘weary of the journey’ (‘wērig’ takes the genitive, ‘sīðes’), and ‘feorrancundum’ ‘come from afar’ (‘feorran’ ‘from afar’ and ‘-cund’ ‘of such origin’), both datives agreeing with ‘him’. ‘seleþegn’ is ‘hall-thane’, a retainer in charge of the hall, the subject of ‘wīsade’, ‘guided’, with ‘forð’ ‘forth’; ‘sē’ is ‘who’, the same man. ‘for andrysnum’ is ‘out of courtesies’ (‘andrysne’, ‘courtesy, respect’, a dative plural after ‘for’). Klaeber’s italic ‘d’ in ‘beweotede’ marks his emendation: the manuscript has ‘be weotene’, and the apparatus credits ‘beweotede’ to Kemble and to Grundtvig (‘Gru. tr.’), the past of ‘beweotian’, ‘attend to, provide for’. ‘ealle … þegnes þearfe’ is ‘all a thane’s need’. ‘swylce’ is ‘such as’, ‘þȳ dōgọre’ a dative of time, ‘on that day’ (or ‘in those days’), ‘heaþolīðende’ ‘battle-sailers’ (‘heaþo’ ‘battle’ and ‘līðende’ ‘sailing, travelling ones’, here warriors who came by sea), and ‘habban scoldon’ ‘had to have’. The dot under the ‘ọ’ of ‘dōgọre’ is the sign explained at 1747. The apparatus adds that the final ‘e’ of the manuscript word is in another hand (doubtful), and that Sievers, Holthausen and Weyhe print ‘dōgor’.

sentences.t: Reste hine þā rūmheort;
sentences.l: Rested himself then the roomy-hearted one;
sentences.i: Then the large-hearted man laid himself to rest;
sentences.n: ‘Reste’ is the past of ‘restan’, ‘rest’, with the reflexive ‘hine’, and the subject is the Geat, not named. ‘rūmheort’ is ‘roomy-hearted’ (‘rūm’ ‘spacious’ and ‘heort’ ‘heart’), which can mean ‘generous’ or ‘at ease’; which is meant is a guess.

sentences.t:
reced hlīuade
gēap ond goldfāh;
sentences.l: the hall towered, wide and gold-gleaming;
sentences.i: the hall towered, broad and bright with gold;
sentences.n: ‘reced’ is ‘hall’ (the house; the same word names Heorot), ‘hlīuade’ the past of ‘hlīfian’, ‘tower, rise high’ (‘hlīfade’ at 81), and ‘gēap’ ‘wide, spacious’, as in ‘horngēap’ at 82, ‘wide between its gable-horns’. ‘goldfāh’ is ‘gold-gleaming’ (‘gold’ and ‘fāh’ ‘coloured, bright’), as at 308.

sentences.t:
gæst inne swæf,
oþ þæt hrefn blaca heofones wynne
blīðheort bodode.
sentences.l: the guest slept within, until the black raven, blithe-hearted, announced the joy of heaven.
sentences.i: the guest slept within until the black raven, glad at heart, announced the joy of heaven.
sentences.n: ‘gæst’ with short ‘æ’ is ‘guest’ (not ‘gāst’, ‘spirit’), the Geat. ‘inne’ is ‘within’, ‘swæf’ the past of ‘swefan’, ‘sleep’ (the verb of 1741). ‘oþ þæt’ is ‘until’; ‘hrefn blaca’ is ‘the black raven’, ‘blaca’ a weak adjective, and it is the subject of ‘bodode’, ‘announced’ (from ‘bodian’), with ‘blīðheort’ ‘blithe-hearted’. ‘heofones wynne’ is its object, ‘the joy of heaven’; I take it to be the daylight or the rising sun, which is a guess, as the text gives no more.

sentences.t:
Ðā cōm beorht scacan
[scīma ofer sceadwa];
sentences.l: Then came, hastening, bright [a gleam over the shadows];
sentences.i: Then the bright light came hastening over the shadows;
sentences.n: ‘cōm … scacan’ is ‘came hastening’, ‘scacan’ an infinitive of ‘scacan’, ‘hasten, shake’, after a verb of motion (as ‘cōmon … gongan’ at 1640–1642), and ‘beorht’ is ‘bright’. The words in brackets are Klaeber’s: the manuscript reads ‘ða com beorht scacan scaþan onetton’ with a half-line missing, and each editor fills the gap differently. Grein supplies ‘lēoma’ or ‘lēoman’ (‘ray’), Heyne ‘sunne’ and ‘ofer grundas’, Sievers and three others ‘scīma æfter sceadwe’, Sedgefield ‘scīma scynded’; Klaeber supplies ‘scīma ofer sceadwa’, ‘a gleam over the shadows’ (‘scīma’ ‘gleam’, ‘sceadwa’ an accusative plural of ‘sceadu’, ‘shadow’). The sense, daybreak, comes from the surrounding words; the exact words are conjecture. The semicolon follows the closing bracket. The apparatus marks the start of a new manuscript leaf (fol. 169b) at ‘ða com’, citing the siglum ‘B’ (I take this to be a Thorkelin transcript).

sentences.l: the warriors hastened, the princes were eager to travel back to their people;
sentences.i: the warriors hurried on, the princes eager to go back to their own people;
sentences.n: ‘scaþan’ is a nominative plural of ‘scaþa’, which in the poem is ‘foe, ravager’ (as in ‘mānscaða’); here it must be said of the Geats as armed men, ‘warriors’, and that sense is a guess from the context. ‘ōnetton’ is the plural past of ‘ōnettan’, ‘hasten’. ‘wǣron … fūse’ is ‘were eager’ (‘fūs’ ‘ready, eager’, as at 1475), ‘æþelingas’ ‘princes’ and ‘eft tō lēodum’ ‘back to the people’. ‘tō farenne’ is an inflected infinitive, ‘to travel’; Klaeber’s italic second ‘n’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘farene ne’, as two words, and Kemble’s ‘farenne’ is the reading printed.

sentences.t:
wolde feor þanon
cuma collenferhð cēoles nēosan.
sentences.l: the newcomer, swollen-minded, wished, far from there, to seek the ship.
sentences.i: The stranger, bold of heart, wished to go far from there and seek his ship.
sentences.n: ‘wolde … nēosan’ is ‘wished to seek’, ‘cēoles’ a genitive after ‘nēosan’, ‘of the ship’; ‘feor þanon’ is ‘far from there’, which I attach to the wish, ‘to go far from there and seek the ship’. ‘cuma’ is ‘newcomer, guest’ (from ‘cuman’, ‘come’), the Geat again, and ‘collenferhð’ is ‘swollen-minded’, which I take to mean ‘excited, bold in spirit’; the root of ‘collen-’ is uncertain, so both the form and the sense are guesses.

sentences.t:
Heht þā se hearda Hrunting beran
sunu Ecglāfes, heht his sweord niman,
lēoflīc īren; —
sentences.l: Then the hard one bade Hrunting be borne to the son of Ecglaf, bade him take his sword, the dear iron; —
sentences.i: Then the stern man bade Hrunting be carried to Ecglaf’s son, and bade him take his sword, that beloved blade; —
sentences.n: ‘Heht’ is the past of ‘hātan’, ‘command’, here with an infinitive and an accusative, ‘heht Hrunting beran’, ‘ordered Hrunting to be borne’, and again ‘heht … niman’, ‘ordered (him) to take’. ‘se hearda’ is ‘the hard one’, Beowulf, as ‘the hard one’ at 401. ‘Hrunting’ is the sword Unferth lent for the dive (1455–1472), the one Beowulf said at 1659 had failed him. ‘sunu Ecglāfes’ is Unferth (‘Ecglāfes bearn’ at 499); the form ‘sunu’ is not an unambiguous dative (Grundtvig prints the dative ‘suna’, the apparatus says), but the next lines thank the man for the sword, so I read it as the one to whom it is carried; that is my reading of a loosely built sentence. ‘his sweord’ is the sword that is Unferth’s own, and ‘lēoflīc īren’ ‘dear iron’ (‘īren’ ‘iron’, so ‘sword’) is in apposition. The dash after the semicolon opens an aside that runs to the dash at 1812.

sentences.t:
sægde him þæs lēanes þanc,
cwæð, hē þone gūðwine gōdne tealde,
wīgcræftigne, nales wordum lōg
mēces ecge;
sentences.l: he said thanks to him for that reward, said he reckoned the war-friend good, skilled in war, and not at all with words found fault with the sword’s edge;
sentences.i: He thanked him for the kindness, said he counted him a good war-friend, skilled in war, and found no fault in words with the sword’s edge;
sentences.n: ‘sægde’ is ‘said’, with ‘him’ a dative, ‘to him’, and ‘þæs lēanes’ a genitive, ‘for that reward’; ‘lēan’ is ‘reward, requital’, the word of 1584 (and of ‘endelēan’ at 1692). The apparatus records Müllenhoff’s ‘lǣnes’, ‘loan’, which would suit a lent sword; Klaeber keeps ‘lēanes’. ‘cwæð’ opens indirect speech: ‘hē … tealde’ is ‘that he reckoned’; the weak past singular has one form for indicative and subjunctive, so the mood cannot be told from the form. ‘þone gūðwine’ is ‘the war-friend’ (‘gūð’ ‘battle’ and ‘wine’ ‘friend’), Unferth, the lender, and ‘gōdne’ and ‘wīgcræftigne’ (‘skilled in war’: ‘wīg’ ‘war’ and ‘cræftig’ ‘skilled’) are accusatives agreeing with him. ‘nales’ is ‘not at all’ (as ‘nallas’ at 1719), ‘wordum lōg’ is ‘with words found fault with’, ‘lōg’ the past of ‘lēan’, ‘blame’, and ‘mēces ecge’ a dative, ‘the sword’s edge’: Beowulf blames neither the man nor the blade, though the sword failed him in the mere. The semicolon ends the courtesies and the poet adds his own remark.

sentences.t: þæt wæs mōdig secg. —
sentences.l: that was a high-spirited man. —
sentences.i: That was a man of spirit. —
sentences.n: ‘mōdig’ is ‘high-minded, spirited, brave’ and ‘secg’ ‘man’. This is the poet’s comment, and the second dash closes the aside begun at 1809. The poet does not say whom he means. I take Beowulf, whose courtesy has just been told, though Unferth, named just before, is also possible.

sentences.t:
Ond þā sīðfrome, searwum gearwe
wīgend wǣron;
sentences.l: And then the journey-bold ones, ready in armour, the warriors were;
sentences.i: And then the warriors were eager to be gone, armed and ready;
sentences.n: ‘sīðfrome’ is ‘journey-bold’ (‘sīð’ ‘journey’ and ‘from’ ‘bold, active’, as ‘frome’ at 1641) and ‘searwum gearwe’ ‘ready in armour’ (‘searu’ ‘armour, war-gear’, a dative plural, and ‘gearwe’ ‘ready’); both are nominative plural adjectives for ‘wīgend’, ‘warriors’, with ‘wǣron’ ‘were’. Klaeber’s semicolon after ‘wǣron’ makes ‘Ond þā’ a main clause, ‘and then’. The apparatus says that most editors put a comma there and read a subordinate clause, ‘and when the warriors were ready’, and that the manuscript has a point after ‘wǣron’; Sedgefield omits ‘ond’.

sentences.t:
ēode weorð Denum
æþeling tō yppan, þǣr se ōþer wæs,
hæle hildedēor Hrōðgār grētte.
sentences.l: went, worthy to the Danes, the prince to the high-seat, where the other was; the hero, battle-brave, greeted Hrothgar.
sentences.i: The prince, honoured among the Danes, went to the high seat where the other sat; and the battle-brave hero greeted Hrothgar.
sentences.n: ‘ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’, ‘go’, ‘weorð Denum’ is ‘worthy to the Danes’ (‘weorð’ with a dative, ‘honoured by, dear to’), and ‘æþeling’ is the subject, Beowulf. ‘tō yppan’ is ‘to the high seat’, ‘yppan’ a dative of ‘yppe’, ‘raised place’, where Hrothgar sat; the exact word is a guess. ‘þǣr se ōþer wæs’ is ‘where the other was’, Hrothgar. ‘hildedēor’ is ‘battle-brave’ (‘hild’ ‘battle’ and ‘dēor’ ‘brave, bold’), and ‘hæle’ is Klaeber’s emendation, the italic ‘æ’: the manuscript has ‘helle’, ‘hell’, which cannot be the sense, and Kemble’s ‘hæle’, a nominative singular variant of ‘hæleð’, ‘hero’, is printed. ‘Hrōðgār’ has the same form as subject and as object; because ‘hæle hildedēor’ repeats ‘æþeling’ I take Beowulf as the greeter, as at 1646, where the same words say that he came ‘Hrōðgār grētan’, to greet Hrothgar. The apparatus refers to Ries for the punctuation of 1815–1816.
